lines.text: Fashion design is the art of applying aesthetics, cultural context, and technical skill to create clothing and accessories. The design process begins with research and inspiration — a designer might draw from architecture, nature, art history, street culture, or personal experience to develop a concept. This vision crystallises on the mood board: a curated collage of images, colours, textures, and references that establishes the collection's emotional direction. Sketching translates the concept into garment ideas — designers draw 'flats' (technical front-and-back illustrations) and 'fashion illustrations' (stylised artistic drawings showing movement and attitude). Fabric selection follows: the designer visits textile fairs, orders swatches, and tests how materials behave — their weight, drape, stretch, and colour retention. Pattern making transforms two-dimensional sketches into three-dimensional garments through flat pattern drafting or draping on a dress form. The toile stage tests the design in inexpensive fabric before committing to costly materials. Sampling produces the first complete garment in final fabric — reviewed, adjusted, and approved before production. For ready-to-wear collections, designs are graded across sizes and sent to manufacturers. For couture, each garment is made individually to the client's measurements. British fashion design is globally celebrated for its creativity, eclecticism, and willingness to challenge conventions — qualities nurtured by world-class fashion schools and a culture that values individuality over conformity.

lines.text: Alexander McQueen (1969–2010) is widely considered the greatest British fashion designer of his generation. His shows were theatrical spectacles — models walked through fire, were painted by robots, and wore garments of extraordinary technical complexity. His legacy continues through the house that bears his name.
